title: Ruru and the harmless snake
hookLine: a grieving groom vows to kill every snake he meets, until a harmless one speaks up and teaches him not to harm
carry: ahimsa: not harming is the highest dharma
tomorrow: who bets her sister's freedom on a horse's tail?
last: KRODHA: ANGER IS AN ENEMY WITHIN.

cards: The wedding has been set. The bride, Pramadvara, is out with her friends, and she steps on a snake she doesn't see. It bites her, and she dies.

The groom is Ruru, a young man of the family of the sage Bhrigu. He goes off alone into the forest and weeps. Then a messenger of the gods comes with an offer: she can live again, if he gives her half of his own life.
He gives it. She wakes. They marry.
It could end there, happily. It doesn't.

teach.b: Ruru makes a vow: whenever he sees a snake, he will kill it. He carries a heavy stick and strikes the snakes he finds. One day he comes on an old snake of a kind called a dundubha, and he raises the stick.
The snake speaks. I've done you no harm. Why strike me?
A snake killed my wife, Ruru answers, so I kill snakes.

teach.h: WE'RE NOT THE ONES WHO BITE.
teach.b: The dundubha says: we're not the ones who bite. We share the name snake with them, and nothing else.

Then it tells him who it really is: a sage, cursed to live in this shape until the day it met Ruru. Standing as a man again, the sage teaches him: not harming living beings is the highest dharma. Ahimsa paramo dharmah.
A man of a priestly family should be known for gentleness and forgiveness, not for the stick.
Notice where the Adi Parva puts this: inside the frame of a king trying to burn the snakes, a creature in a snake's shape speaks for ahimsa first. Ruru's grief was real.
But he had turned one bite into a war on a whole kind of creature. That one phrase runs deep in Hindu life.

teach.h: A SPIDER CARRIED OUT IN A CUP.
teach.b: It's a big part of why many Hindu families keep vegetarian kitchens, why a grandmother might carry a spider outside in a cup, and why ahimsa leads the list of restraints in the Yoga Sutras.
The sage even points ahead and says Janamejaya's snake sacrifice was stopped. Then Ruru goes home to ask his father for the rest.

how: Ahimsa, not harming living beings, is taught in Hindu texts beyond this one, and some Hindus practice it through vegetarian diet, care for animals, and restraint in speech.

o: a hymn of thanks for a bride brought back from death

games.q: a friend says: 'a dog bit me once, so i can't stand dogs.' by the dundubha's lesson, what fits?
o: that dog bit you; the others share the name and nothing else.
fair. one bite shows what dogs are like.
dogs are sacred in Hinduism, so you have to love them.
games.why: the dundubha: we share the name snake, and nothing else. then the freed sage teaches that not harming is the highest dharma.

practice: Bring to mind one hurt that came from one person or one thing, and notice whether it has spread: from one dog to all dogs, one driver to all drivers, one person to everyone who looks like them.
Don't argue with it; just see the line between the one that bit and the ones that never did. Breathe in on the one, and out on the many.
